title: NNN and STNL Property Sourcing
name: NNN and STNL Property Sourcing
metaTitle: NNN and STNL Property Sourcing in Denver, CO
metaDescription: Sourcing net lease and single-tenant properties for 1031 exchange buyers along Denver's I-25 and I-70 corridors, from drive-thru pads to corporate ground leases.

sections.html: A lot of exchange investors want to stop managing property altogether after years of handling tenant calls, and a triple net or single-tenant net lease deal is how they get there. Denver's I-25 and I-70 corridors carry a steady supply of these, from drive-thru pads outside big-box centers to freestanding buildings on long corporate leases. We build the sourcing list around what the landlord actually has to do, which in a clean NNN deal is not much.

sections.heading: Where the net lease pads sit
sections.html: The I-25 corridor through the southern suburbs, Parker, Castle Rock, and Highlands Ranch, carries pad sites developed alongside retail centers where a national chain wants a standalone building with drive-thru access. The I-70 corridor east of downtown carries a different mix, quick-service restaurants and auto service tenants serving commuter traffic rather than shopping-center overflow. Both corridors keep adding pads as retail centers redevelop, so the pipeline refreshes regularly instead of drying up.

sections.heading: Corporate versus franchisee leases
sections.html: A lease backed directly by a corporate tenant reads very differently from one backed by a local franchisee operator, even if the building and rent look identical on paper. Corporate leases carry stronger credit and usually longer guarantee terms. Franchisee-backed leases can still work, but we pull the operator's other locations and general reputation before recommending the deal, since a struggling franchisee can walk away from a lease in a way a corporate tenant rarely does.

sections.heading: Ground lease versus fee-simple ownership
sections.html: Some of these pads sell as a ground lease, where the investor owns the land under a tenant-built structure, and some sell fee-simple, where the investor owns land and building together. Ground leases carry lower management burden and often longer terms, but the return is usually thinner. Fee-simple deals carry a bit more responsibility for the building itself but typically price at a better yield. We ask an investor which tradeoff fits their exchange before narrowing the list.

sections.heading: Structures we track most often
sections.html:
The recurring property types in this pipeline include:

  • Drive-thru quick-service restaurant pads with corporate guarantees
  • Freestanding auto service and tire centers on long-term leases
  • Bank branch buildings with ground lease structures
  • Convenience store and fuel center pads along I-25 and I-70 frontage
  • Single-tenant pharmacy buildings with 15-plus year lease terms
  • Urgent care pad sites paired with a corporate operator

sections.heading: What can go wrong after closing
sections.html:
The biggest risk in this asset class isn't the building, it's the lease renewal. A tenant with an option to walk at year ten instead of a hard renewal commitment can leave an investor holding a single-purpose building with a narrow pool of replacement tenants. We check option language and any co-tenancy clauses tied to the anchor center before a pad goes on the identification list.

Rent escalations deserve a close look too. Some net lease deals carry flat rent for the entire primary term, which sounds stable until an investor realizes the real return shrinks every year against inflation and rising property tax. Others build in fixed annual bumps or periodic increases tied to a set schedule. We compare escalation structure across candidates on every list, since two properties with identical starting cap rates can produce very different returns ten years out depending on how rent grows.

sections.heading: Financing considerations for single-tenant deals
sections.html:
Lenders underwrite single-tenant net lease deals largely on the tenant's credit rather than the real estate itself, which cuts both ways for a Denver exchange buyer. A corporate-backed pharmacy or bank branch can get favorable loan terms even in a smaller submarket, since the lender is really betting on the tenant, not the building's location. A franchisee-backed pad in a less established corridor can face tighter terms even with a decent building, since the lender weighs the operator's financial strength more heavily than the real estate underneath it.

We flag that financing gap early, before a property makes the identification list, so an investor isn't caught mid-diligence discovering their preferred lender won't touch a franchisee-backed deal on the terms they expected.

faqs.q: What's the real difference between a corporate-backed and franchisee-backed net lease deal?
faqs.a: Corporate leases carry the parent company's credit behind the rent payment, which lenders and buyers both value higher. Franchisee leases depend on that specific operator's finances, so we check the operator's track record before recommending the property.

faqs.q: Should I buy the ground under a pad or the building itself?
faqs.a: A ground lease means less to manage and often a longer term, but a lower yield. Owning building and land together, known as fee-simple, usually prices better but puts more responsibility on you if the tenant leaves.

faqs.q: How much diligence does a single-tenant net lease deal actually require?
faqs.a: Less than a multi-tenant building, but the lease itself needs a close read. Renewal options, co-tenancy clauses, and any right of first refusal the tenant holds all affect what happens if that tenant eventually leaves.

faqs.q: Are I-25 corridor pads more expensive than I-70 corridor pads?
faqs.a: Generally yes, since I-25 pads sit closer to higher-income southern suburbs and denser retail centers. I-70 corridor pads can offer a better basis if the tenant and lease terms still check out.

faqs.q: What happens to a single-tenant building if the tenant doesn't renew?
faqs.a: The building often needs retrofitting for a new tenant since it was built to one operator's specifications. We flag that risk during sourcing so the identification list doesn't lean too heavily on properties with weak renewal language.
